Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off. Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead. I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times (NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe. Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company. Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment. In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post, "Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." Although President Trump's remarks sound promising, this does not mark the end of government scrutiny. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Commerce Department are conducting a criminal export-control investigation into Singapore-based Megaspeed. The objective of this investigation is to determine whether Nvidia's artificial intelligence (AI) chips were diverted through Megaspeed to Chinese companies and China's state-owned military contractors. As confirmed by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, Alice Huang is directly under investigation as part of this probe. While the Justice Department recently stated it found no evidence of wrongdoing by Jensen Huang regarding his relationship with Alice Huang, federal prosecutors are still investigating her former firm, Megaspeed, over potential export-control violations. In addition, on December 1, Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear before the House Intelligence Committee, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Select Committee on China. Beyond the regulatory threats Nvidia faces, I believe investor sentiment toward the company is likely to remain weak, given ongoing scrutiny of aggressive AI investments by hyperscalers and tech giants. The biggest macro risk is that AI investments are outpacing earnings. A quick look at hyperscalers' EBITDA and capex reveals why investors are worried. According to Morningstar (MORN) data, capex as a percentage of EBITDA among Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN), Meta Platforms, Inc. (META), Alphabet Inc. (GOOG), and Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) averaged just 43% in 2024. This ratio ballooned to 60% in 2025, with estimates pointing to a further expansion of this ratio to 90% this year. At the same time, Morningstar expects the incremental EBITDA yield on prior-year capex to fall from 50% in 2025 to 39% in 2026, underscoring that earnings realization is lagging behind capital deployment. These projections suggest that hyperscalers are spending heavily on AI with the expectation of fully realizing the returns only over the longer term. Massive upfront outlays for chips, data centers, and power infrastructure will continue to pressure free cash flows (FCFs) and push big tech companies to issue more debt. That dynamic does not bode well for Nvidia, as any move by hyperscalers to moderate spending to protect FCF would directly hit the chipmaker's revenue. Nvidia is currently valued at a forward P/E multiple of just 16x. That is well below its five-year average of 40.99x. The multiple looks cheap for a company that nearly doubled revenue over the 12 months ended October 31. I believe this seemingly cheap valuation is a classic cyclical trap rather than a bargain today. My caution centers on three specific risks. First, the active SEC review into accounting practices and geographic revenue disclosures creates unquantifiable legal and restatement risk. Second, a slowdown in hyperscaler AI spending will compress forward EPS estimates for Nvidia meaningfully. Third, increased scrutiny on chip exports may deteriorate investor sentiment before we see an improvement. Until regulators clarify disclosure questions and hyperscaler return on invested capital proves durable without vendor-financing support, I prefer waiting for clearer earnings visibility before adding to my position. Based on the ratings of 44 Wall Street analysts, the average Nvidia price target is $234, which implies upside of roughly 57% from the current market price, according to TipRanks data. Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO on November 23 sent its stock higher, as expected. Contrary to popular belief, I believe CEO Huang's return to the company does not solve the regulatory threats faced by the company. In fact, I believe regulatory scrutiny will only increase with his return as CEO. Nvidia is entering a period of legal chaos at a time when investors are questioning the durability of aggressive AI spending by hyperscalers. Together, these challenges are likely to keep Nvidia stock under pressure in the foreseeable future. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

Two Sigma Investments, once directly run by billionaire John Overdeck, reported holding 10,481,406 shares of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), worth $2.39 billion, as of Sept. 30, 2026, in its Nov. 16 13F filing. As of June 30, the fund held 6,284,574 shares, so its share count rose 66.8% in one quarter. The increase makes a strong headline. Read closely, the filing reveals far less about the fund’s thinking than the headline suggests. Is NVIDIA a Buy After Jensen Huang's Shocking Exit? Plus New Robotics Stock Buys Nvidia is Two Sigma’s largest long stock position. It still makes up only 1.74% of $137.68 billion in reported long positions spread across 3,877 stocks. Two Sigma is a quantitative, multi-strategy firm associated with founders Overdeck and Siegel. It runs systematic, model-driven strategies, and its wide-based book covers risk lightly by design, so a conviction investor’s top holding often represents a large piece of the fund. At Two Sigma, the largest stock holding represents a small share of its disclosed long-stock portfolio, rather than its total assets or overall investment exposure. Alongside the Nvidia shares, the filing lists both call options and put options. A call option gains value when the stock rises, so it is a bullish position. A put option gains value when the stock falls, so it is a bearish position. A 13F reports only the underlying shares for these rows. The premium paid, the strike price, and the expiration date are all undisclosed, so the real size and purpose of the options are unknown. A retail investor reading the filing sees a fund holding positions on both sides of the same stock, with no way to tell which side carries more weight. 13F holdings are reported roughly 45 days after quarter-end, and every value reflects prices on Sept. 30. The filing gives no reasons, shows no trade dates, and says nothing about what Two Sigma holds today. That gap matters here. Nvidia shares fell 30.88% over the past month to $149.30, so the market today looks very different from the one in the filing. The fundamental picture that retirement investors can verify sits in Nvidia’s own disclosures. Third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue reached $115.844 billion[1], up 103.21%, and non-GAAP EPS of $2.68 exceeded the $2.4712 consensus. Nvidia also faces governance risks following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, an ongoing independent board investigation, and $390 billion in supply commitments. For a retirement-focused investor, Two Sigma’s Nvidia increase is a poor signal. A systematic fund trades on model outputs across thousands of names, rebalances often, and holds options whose direction and size the filing does not reveal. The 66.8% increase confirms that Nvidia carried more weight in the fund on Sept. 30 than on June 30, and the filing confirms nothing beyond that. Nvidia’s own earnings reports, guidance, and risk disclosures give investors a firmer basis for a decision (we studied what the early signals of the biggest tech winners looked like, Nvidia included, in a free playbook here). "It is critical to put this electoral shift into operational context. In my view, this is not going to completely stop data center construction in the United States—the underlying structural demand for compute is far too massive. However, it forces big tech hyperscalers and infrastructure developers to pull up a chair to the negotiating table with local Democratic administrations and utility regulators. This creates a brand-new layer of regulatory friction, permitting delays, and energy tariff reviews that will inevitably slow down the overall growth rate of data center buildouts for the foreseeable future." That exact operational dynamic shows up in Morgan Stanley’s latest CapEx trajectory below: total spending keeps climbing, yet the pace of expansion hits a sharp wall in 2028. As we can see, hyperscaler CapEx will keep growing through 2028, reaching a total of $1.76T; however, the stocks of companies that depend on that massive hyperscaler demand—such as Nvidia $NVDA , neoclouds like CoreWeave $CRWV and Nebius $NBIS, as well as players across adjacent sectors like power and grid infrastructure, cooling, data-center construction, and optical networking/interconnects—base their current share prices on the future growth rate of that demand. My November 18 post on Nvidia—"NVIDIA — After a 36% Drop from All-Time Highs: The Structural Factors Its New CEO Must Focus On"—which has been very well received by the community, lays out the different challenges the company faces ahead even with Jensen Huang back as CEO. And my October 23 post, "Inside the Neocloud Trap: What CoreWeave, Nebius, and the AI Gold Rush Are Hiding," also very well received by the community, details precisely that dependence on hyperscalers. That is why both posts are complementary to this one: here we can see how future demand is estimated across all the companies and sectors that depend on hyperscaler CapEx spending. Now let’s look closely at what is happening with those growth estimates over the coming years. Look at the right-hand chart, "Hyperscaler CapEx Growth," and see how at the end of 2025, 2026 CapEx growth was projected around 60%, before successive revisions across April, July, September, and November 2026 pushed this year’s growth rate all the way to 98%. Likewise, those same late-2025 estimates projected roughly 20% CapEx growth for 2027, only for subsequent updates across April, July, September, and November 2026 to lift 2027 growth to 73%. The real concern shows up in 2028: late-2025 estimates started near 0% growth, and earlier revisions—such as April and September 2026—only lifted the projected growth rate to 7%, with the latest November 2026 update failing to add any meaningful upward push to that pace. That is an atypical pattern compared with 2026 and 2027, and it creates an asymmetric risk: without fresh upward revisions supporting the CapEx trajectory, the probability of downward revisions rises substantially if physical bottlenecks, permitting delays, or financing constraints intensify. Taken together, this points to CapEx growth hitting a ceiling around 2028—even as total dollar spending remains elevated. Share prices depend on future revenue growth, which in turn depends on future demand for a company’s products and services. If that demand slows down, stock prices are going to experience significant volatility over the coming quarters. Investors in these sectors need to watch closely what other business lines are driving companies like Nvidia, neoclouds, and adjacent suppliers—and how effectively they can pivot to offset a potential future deceleration in hyperscaler spending. NVIDIA — After a 36% Drop from All-Time Highs: The Structural Factors Its New CEO Must Focus On Yesterday, Nvidia $NVDA reported extraordinary financial results for its fiscal third quarter: record revenues of $115.8 billion (up 103% year-over-year, with Data Center revenue reaching $107.6 billion) and a net income of $65.3 billion, crushing Wall Street expectations in its first earnings report under interim CEO Colette Kress. Wall Street views this—alongside a bullish $130 billion Q4 revenue outlook—as absolute proof that the revenue machine is running at full throttle. However, as Nvidia enters this new leadership chapter following the departure of Jensen Huang, the incoming CEO will have to navigate a far more fragile architectural reality: direct sales to hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta) account for 50% to 55% of Nvidia’s total revenue—and when you factor in the indirect sales channeled through the rest of the ecosystem, the true dependency on these cloud giants is even higher. With such heavy exposure to just a handful of hyperscalers, any strategic shift, budget cut, or architectural pivot on their part can significantly alter Nvidia’s future growth trajectory. Beyond these headline figures, the vast majority of Nvidia's ecosystem investments continue to flow directly through their infrastructure, masking deep structural vulnerabilities behind short-term demand. To explore these potential vulnerabilities in Nvidia's GPU demand, we must examine the different subsectors in which Nvidia has invested (the first step before deciding whether to invest or not is always to map out the underlying architecture and understand where we truly stand). Section 1: Subsectors Where Nvidia Is Deploying Its Capital Before breaking down Nvidia’s portfolio investments, it is critical to note a major shift already reshaping cloud demand: inference has overtaken training, now accounting for 55% to 65% of total AI cloud compute. While frontier model training required massive, densely interconnected clusters where Nvidia’s GPUs and CUDA software were indispensable—due to the raw parallel processing power needed to build models from scratch—the industry is maturing toward high-volume inference, which simply means running already-trained models to answer daily user queries at scale. This transition is about to accelerate sharply due to a new physical and regulatory bottleneck driven directly by recent U.S. midterm election outcomes. Across battleground states, voters pushed back aggressively against soaring household electricity bills and grid strain caused by massive AI data centers. Democratic candidates capitalized on this exact mandate—campaigning on strict legislative moratoria, mandatory grid impact audits, and rigorous utility permitting reviews to protect local ratepayers. When hyperscalers face strict caps and delays on how many new power-hungry data centers they can plug into the grid, they can no longer expand brute-force training capacity at will; instead, they are forced to maximize output per watt from existing infrastructure—accelerating the shift toward standardized inference where their own custom silicon (ASICs) excels. For a deeper analysis of how these electoral shifts and grid constraints are slowing down data center expansion, readers can consult my post published on November 6, 2026: Behind the Market Crash: The Real Drivers of the Massive Tech and Semiconductor Sell-Off — And Who Will Emerge as the True Winners? (November 6, 2026). With this structural shift in mind, let’s analyze the core subsectors where Nvidia has invested to uncover their underlying vulnerabilities. Subsector 1: Nvidia's investments in Neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, Nscale) Nvidia backs specialized GPU cloud providers—known as "neoclouds"—with both equity and preferential chip allocations so these firms can build out AI data centers at breakneck speed. On paper, neoclouds look like a new, independent class of major hardware buyers that reduce Nvidia’s reliance on the hyperscalers. In practice, neoclouds operate primarily as overflow capacity subcontractors for the hyperscalers themselves—for instance, Microsoft has relied heavily on multi-billion-dollar contracts with CoreWeave to bridge its own short-term data center bottlenecks. The Result: This segment represents fragile, cyclical demand for Nvidia. Neoclouds do not control the end-enterprise customer relationship, and their business model depends on hyperscalers facing temporary capacity shortages. As AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud finish building their own data centers, those hyperscalers have every financial incentive to pull those workloads back in-house rather than pay a middleman markup—leaving neocloud utilization, and their future GPU orders, highly vulnerable. Vulnerability for Nvidia: High. Neoclouds rely on debt-financed expansion and temporary capacity bottlenecks at the hyperscalers. While skeptics might argue that hyperscalers will simply buy the GPUs that neoclouds stop ordering once workloads move in-house, that transfer is not a one-for-one replacement: as workloads shift from model training to inference, Nvidia's GPUs will become less necessary because hyperscalers will rely more on their own custom chips for these models. For more details on this subsector, readers can consult my post published on October 23: Inside the Neocloud Trap: What CoreWeave, Nebius, and the AI Gold Rush Are Hiding (October 23). Subsector 2: Nvidia's investments in Foundation Model Labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Mistral) Nvidia invests billions of dollars directly into AI model labs—such as OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Mistral—so that these companies use that capital to buy or rent Nvidia GPUs. On the surface, this makes Wall Street believe that demand for Nvidia’s chips is diversifying beyond the hyperscalers. The reality, however, is that these AI labs do not own hyperscale data centers. When OpenAI, Anthropic, or Mistral receive that cash from Nvidia and venture backers, they turn around and spend it on massive multi-year cloud commitments with the hyperscalers (Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud) to rent the compute capacity needed to train and run their models. The Result: Even though these AI labs route their capital through the hyperscalers' infrastructure, Nvidia’s position in frontier model training remains resilient for now due to deep developer entrenchment in the CUDA software ecosystem and superior NVLink interconnect speeds. However, as the broader AI market shifts away from heavy model training and toward high-volume, cost-sensitive inference, the nature of demand changes entirely. In this new phase, hyperscalers no longer depend on Nvidia's training moats; instead, hyperscalers are aggressively deploying their own custom ASICs (such as Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium) to handle standardized inference workloads in-house, bypassing Nvidia entirely and destroying future GPU demand. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Low in Training / High in Inference Transition. While frontier model training remains anchored to Nvidia hardware due to high technical friction and CUDA lock-in, the industry's inevitable maturation toward scaled inference strips away that protection. As workloads shift away from training, hyperscalers hold all the leverage to route traffic through their own cost-efficient silicon—directly cannibalizing Nvidia's future revenue growth. Subsector 3: Nvidia's investments in AI Software & Vertical Applications (Perplexity AI, Harvey, SoundHound) Nvidia deploys venture capital into AI software startups and vertical applications—such as Perplexity AI in conversational search, Harvey in legal AI, and SoundHound in voice AI—to stimulate end-market adoption of artificial intelligence. Unlike cloud providers, however, these software companies do not buy physical GPUs from Nvidia or build their own data centers. Instead, they use their venture funding to rent cloud compute and API capacity directly from the hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud) to run their applications for end users. The Result: This layer generates strictly indirect demand that funnels straight back into the hyperscalers' infrastructure, concentrating buying power in the exact same three or four cloud giants. Furthermore, while training is protected by CUDA, enterprise and consumer software applications generate primarily high-volume inference workloads—answering user queries in real time rather than training models from scratch. Because software-level abstraction removes CUDA lock-in at the application layer, hyperscalers can steadily migrate this inference traffic onto their own lower-cost custom ASICs without disrupting the end user—gradually eroding Nvidia’s share of incremental compute growth. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Moderate. While seeding software applications successfully expands overall AI compute demand, these workloads consist predominantly of standardized inference rather than complex model training. As workloads shift from model training to inference, Nvidia's GPUs will become less necessary because hyperscalers will rely more on their own custom chips for these models. Subsector 4: Nvidia's investments in Autonomous Vehicles, Robotics & Physical AI (Figure AI, Serve Robotics, Wayve, WeRide) Nvidia also deploys capital into autonomous vehicles, humanoid robotics, and "Physical AI" startups—such as Figure AI, Serve Robotics, Wayve, and WeRide—to establish its hardware and software stack as the foundational operating system for machines operating in the physical world. Unlike cloud software or foundation model labs, these companies do not rely on hyperscaler data centers to execute their core workloads; instead, they require real-time, low-latency onboard inference directly at the edge (powered by Nvidia DRIVE and Jetson chips) alongside physics-accurate digital twin simulations (via Nvidia Omniverse and Isaac). The Result: This is one of the few ecosystem segments where demand does not funnel back through AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud. While Alphabet and Amazon operate closed, proprietary robotaxi subsidiaries (Waymo and Zoox, respectively), neither they nor Microsoft or Meta commercialize horizontal edge-computing chips or physical simulation platforms for third-party automakers and robotics developers. Consequently, hyperscalers cannot cannibalize this workload with their cloud-centric custom ASICs, allowing Nvidia to capture an end-to-end moat—from simulation training in the lab to embedded inference inside the vehicle or robot itself. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Low to Moderate. Nvidia maintains a genuine architectural advantage here because hyperscalers do not compete as B2B silicon suppliers at the physical edge. The vulnerability is only moderate insofar as commercial adoption timelines for autonomous fleets and humanoid robotics remain multi-year capital cycles that are still too small today to offset a near-term slowdown in massive data center GPU orders. Section 2: Do Nvidia's Investments in These Subsectors Actually Impact Its Bottom Line? Wall Street loves to treat Nvidia's web of minority equity stakes across neoclouds, model labs, and software startups as proof of a self-sustaining, diversified ecosystem. A basic financial reality check shows why this narrative falls apart. The investments that Nvidia holds in these subsectors experience valuation shifts. Under U.S. accounting rules (ASC 321), any appreciation or depreciation in those stakes is included directly in Nvidia’s Income Statement, meaning they have a direct impact on its net income. However, looking at the numbers as of September 2026, that "other income, net" account was barely 8.7% of total revenues during the first nine months of the year. While these paper gains pad the bottom line, they pale in comparison to Nvidia's massive core hardware revenues. More importantly, the incoming CEO will need to closely monitor the vulnerable subsectors we outlined above. If growth in those fragile segments decelerates, it won't just trigger negative valuation adjustments flowing into the income statement—it will serve as the canary in the coal mine. A slowdown among those startups means their hardware purchases are drying up, exposing the core risk: many of these companies only bought Nvidia GPUs in the first place because Nvidia injected the capital right back into them. The sole objective of this post is neither to be bullish nor bearish, but rather to analyze Nvidia's architecture and core ecosystem sectors to understand where we currently stand and what underlying trends are emerging. Looking at what we have examined, it is critical to assess whether the company's massive past growth will be sustainable over the next 5 to 10 years. Going forward, it is essential to monitor how the interim CEO—and whoever follows—addresses Nvidia's vulnerable points while adapting the business to the rising dominance of inference models and a slower-growth data center environment shaped by the implementation of the new legislative agenda following recent elections. From a personal capital allocation standpoint, I am not initiating a new position just yet—I still need to see how the new leadership executes its strategy to sustain the business through these structural shifts. Naturally, if I had bought my shares two or three years ago, I would sit on enough margin of safety to comfortably hold through this transition. Notably, according to TIKR Terminal, Nvidia is currently trading at its lowest EV/EBIT multiple in five years. Ultimately, however, whether this represents an opportunity comes down to each investor’s individual risk profile; in my case, seeing such heavy concentration in a handful of hyperscalers keeps me firmly on the sidelines. Clear catalysts are still needed, because a stock that looks cheap can often remain cheap for a long time—and the structural shifts outlined in this post indicate that the incoming CEO will need near-flawless execution across multiple fronts of the business to replicate the extraordinary growth the company has delivered over the past few years across the next five. This type of structural analysis is not a theoretical exercise: it is the only way to avoid destroying your capital in companies that the market assumes are infallible. CFO and interim-CEO Colette Kress said it's "business as usual" at Nvidia, painting an optimistic picture on the company's earnings call. So, with the stock trading at a level rarely seen in the past year, should investors consider buying the stock? Warren Buffett's long-held investment philosophy can provide the answer to that question. Many investors might look at Nvidia's drop and think, "The market is fearful; I should get greedy." After all, Kress just increased her guidance for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. Wall Street analysts see Nvidia's earnings per share climbing above $16 next year. The stock trades at ridiculously low multiples. While it's true that Buffett has long noted that one of the keys to his success as an investor is "to be greedy only when others are fearful," that's not the only requirement for a good investment. Buffett also only invested in stocks when he had a high degree of confidence in their future. If a company was deemed too difficult to understand or forecast, he stayed away. "Investors should remember that their scorecard is not computed using Olympic-diving methods: Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count," Buffett wrote in his 1994 letter to Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA) (NYSE:BRKB) shareholders. "If you are right about a business whose value is largely dependent on a single key factor that is both easy to understand and enduring, the payoff is the same as if you had correctly analyzed an investment alternative characterized by many constantly shifting and complex variables." At this point, Nvidia's business is more like the latter than the former. Huang's actions and the potential repercussions leave many unanswered questions for investors. The high level of uncertainty about Nvidia's future explains why it trades at such a low multiple. It's not fear; it's a rational response to the recent events impacting the company. There are a couple of alternatives to Nvidia stock trading at earnings multiples that aren't much higher than the chip leader. Buffett himself initiated a position in Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) in 2025. His thesis was based on the company's ability to deploy huge sums of capital with a high return on investment. Specifically, Buffett was talking about its Google Cloud Platform and its data centers full of GPUs and custom silicon. Alphabet is well-positioned to deliver high returns on invested capital in Google Cloud because of its full-stack approach to AI. It designs the systems and chips in its data centers; it offers a full cloud platform for developers (not just infrastructure); it develops a frontier large language model; and it integrates AI capabilities across its products. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that its payback period for the average server in its data centers is just two years, and its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems break even within half that time. With a useful life of six years and a good operating margin, that's an exceptional return on invested capital. That return on invested capital is set to climb as more spending shifts from data center shells to revenue-generating servers. Another company positioned to grow based on a single key factor is Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). Broadcom is the leading custom AI accelerator design partner, the one Alphabet uses for most of its TPUs. Growing demand for custom silicon, which costs less up front than GPUs and offers better price-performance, should result in its AI chip revenue climbing faster than the competition's for years to come. Its lead is protected by its intellectual property and its close relationship with its foundry partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. While Nvidia currently trades around 16 times earnings expectations, Broadcom's stock price isn't much higher at 17 times forward earnings. Alphabet is more expensive at 21 times forward earnings, but it's arguably the least risky of the group, considering its digital advertising business remains a huge cash cow funding its growth. title: Buyer beware? Nvidia's volatile swings expose risks of single-stock ETFs - CNBC
content:
Nvidia’s latest bout of volatility is highlighting risks tied to single-stock exchange-traded funds. Among the hardest hit: the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF (NVD). The fund sank 63% on Monday after Jensen Huang got reinstated as the chip giant’s CEO. Meanwhile, the firm’s 2x Long NVDA ETF (NVDL) soared nearly 62% on the same day. ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins joined “ETF Edge” as Nvidia shares soared 31% during Monday’s session, wiping a large portion of the losses from the days following Huang’s resignation. Shares cooled on Tuesday and Wednesday, however. “Historically speaking, we do not see these types of large drawdowns followed by huge drives up in a healthy market,” Akins said on Monday. “It usually tends to be when you’re in a recession or in a bear market territory, which we’re not technically in for the broader market, but we are in for this AI trade.” But it may not be time to go cold turkey on single-stock funds. ″[Leveraged ETFs are] definitely a retail trading vehicle…  I think it’s OK to have a little fun trying to trade that,” Akins added. “I’m certain there are people that are better at trading these than others. But on the whole, timing the market is very, very hard.” GraniteShares founder and CEO Will Rhind also joined “ETF Edge” on Monday as Nvidia single-stock short ETFs overshadowed his firm’s new Anthropic launches: The 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF (ANS) and the 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF (AIL). “We thought this was going to be the biggest news event of the day with Anthropic the first leveraged ETFs going live,” he said. “I can tell you this is like a sideshow compared to what we’re seeing with Nvidia.” Rhind suggests Nvidia’s wild swings aren’t dampening enthusiasm for single-stock ETFs. “As long as there’s enthusiasm in the underlying name… people will want to trade it and most likely want to trade it with leverage either on the long on the short side,” added Rhind. “Fast Money” tackled the risks tied to ETFs that are tied to single stocks, too. “If this is somehow part of a portfolio, [then] that is a dangerous game to be playing,” trader Guy Adami said on Monday. Karen Finerman also addressed the strategy’s downsides. “Leverage is always the thing that kills. It’s always leverage,” said Finerman, co-founder and CEO of Metropolitan Capital Advisors, in the same interview. “You can survive anything but leverage.” As of Wednesday’s close, the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF plunged 55% so far this week while the GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF is up 31%. title: Does S&P’s Credit Warning Matter For Nvidia Stock? - Trefis
content: S&P Global Ratings put Nvidia on CreditWatch with negative implications on Wednesday, Nov 25. That is a formal warning that it could cut Nvidia’s credit rating. A credit rating is a grade on how safely a company can repay what it borrows. S&P cited rising management and governance risk, not money trouble. The short answer is that a cut has very little to bite on. A lower rating mainly raises what a company pays to borrow. Nvidia holds more cash than it owes. At the latest quarter in our data, which ended Jul 26, 2026, it held $62.5 billion of cash and short-term investments. Nvidia has since reported its October quarter, but those figures are not yet in our data. Its total debt was $38.4 billion. That leaves Nvidia with $24.1 billion more cash than debt. Over the four quarters to Jul 26, it paid $463 million of interest. Its operating cash flow, the cash the business itself brought in, was $134.4 billion. That covered the interest bill about 290 times. In the latest quarter, Nvidia even earned more interest on its cash than it paid on its debt. The stock is a different story. It closed at $149.30 on Wednesday, down 3.9% on the day. That is 37.6% below its Oct 6 close of $239.24. For this week’s slide, see Did Nvidia Stock Fall On Its Own? Nvidia stock has already fallen 37.6% from its Oct 6 high. A fall that deep is hard to sit through when your savings have to cover the bills. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays. S&P’s concern is about people and oversight. The board recently reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. S&P said news about the CEO and questions about export controls exposed weak spots in how Nvidia is managed and governed. It singled out the board. None of that is a claim about cash or debt. So the warning is about who runs the company, not whether it can pay. A rating cut on these grounds would not change what Nvidia owns or owes. The table below sets Nvidia next to four other large tech companies. It shows each one’s debt against its cash, and how many times its operating cash covered its interest bill. Debt is total debt at each company’s latest reported quarter. Cash means cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments on the same date. Interest cover is operating cash flow over the four quarters to that date, divided by interest paid in the same four quarters. Broadcom leans on debt the most. It owed $35.4 billion more than its cash and short-term investments. Its interest took 7.7 cents of each dollar of operating cash. Nvidia’s interest cover was 22.2 times Broadcom’s. Advanced Micro Devices carries a little less debt per dollar of cash than Nvidia. Its cash covered its interest 53.0 times. Microsoft covered its interest 60.8 times. Apple owed $23.4 billion more than its cash and short-term investments. Its interest bill is not in our data, so we cannot measure its cover. Of the four with data, Nvidia’s cash covered its interest by far the most times. The other side of the ledger is that Nvidia is borrowing more. Its total debt grew 261.9% in the year to Jul 26, from $10.6 billion. It issued $24.9 billion of new debt in the six months to that date. Its interest bill grew with it. Interest in the quarter to Jul 26 was 3.7 times the same quarter a year earlier. Its cash cushion over debt shrank by $19.3 billion in that year. A stricter count gives a less comfortable picture. It leaves out leases and short-term investments, and sets debt against cash alone. On that count Nvidia owed $10.9 billion more than its cash. Even so, the bill stays small. If the latest quarter’s interest repeated for four quarters, it would come to $908 million a year. That is 0.68% of Nvidia’s operating cash over the four quarters to Jul 26. Our data runs only to that quarter, so a full quarter of interest on the new debt is not yet in it. Nvidia also held $51.2 billion of long-term investments and advances, outside the cash figure. Whether those holdings are safe is a separate question from this rating. Our read: a rating cut would raise what Nvidia pays to borrow, and that bill is small next to its cash flow. The risk S&P names is about the board and management. Those are risks a shareholder already carries by owning the stock. Two things would change that view. One is the next balance sheet showing debt again rising much faster than cash, as it did in the year to Jul 26. The other is the governance worry hurting sales or cash flow. This question is part of our wider AI storyline. A strong balance sheet did not stop a 37.6% fall since Oct 6. Some companies don't forecast that far into the future because visibility that far out is hard to achieve. But with the industry in a supply-constrained state, it's easier for Nvidia to estimate how many chips it will be able to sell. Nvidia looks set to have another year of solid growth in 2028, although a 75% clip again likely won't be in the cards. Thanks to the turmoil surrounding the leadership transition, Nvidia's stock now trades at a dirt cheap 16.6 times trailing earnings. I don't think that's a reasonable price for the stock to trade at, as I think a 30x valuation is far more reasonable, given its market position and growth prospects. Wall Street analysts estimate Nvidia will generate around $424 billion in its next fiscal year. Assuming management's 75% growth rate is accurate, that brings its total to $742 billion. Over the past 12 months, Nvidia's profit margin has eclipsed 60%, but I'll set it at 60% to bake in a bit of conservatism. That would mean Nvidia will generate around $445 billion in profits. If we assume Nvidia can grow at an additional 20% year-over-year pace in 2028 (which is Nvidia's fiscal 2029), that would bring its profit total to $534 billion. content: Nvidia's stock is the cheapest it has been since the financial crisis Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) stock has had a busy few weeks. It was heavily affected by the resignation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, and questions are now surfacing about how much of Nvidia's sales were conducted legally and whether any of its chips ended up in China. Huang is now back as CEO, but there is no definitive answer on export issues, and the market isn't sticking around to find out the conclusion of this saga. Instead, it has sold off Nvidia's stock to a point not seen in years. In fact, with its stock closing at about $125 per share on Friday, it's traded at a price not seen since May 2025. After Huang returned, the stock rose to around $155 per share. Nvidia stock hasn’t been priced this low since mid-2025. However, Nvidia has grown significantly as a company since then, making its valuation cheap. But just how cheap is it? Let's take a look. First, let's look at how Nvidia is trading based on trailing earnings. For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) trades at 20.3 times trailing earnings. As of the price Nvidia closed at on Nov. 24, the stock trades at just 16.7 times earnings. That type of discount is normally reserved for companies with major business problems or those operating in deeply cyclical industries. While Nvidia may operate in a cyclical industry, the reality is that the artificial intelligence build-out isn't wrapping up anytime soon, and there will always be a need to replace outdated or burnt-out equipment. However, the trailing price-to-earnings ratio is a bad metric for Nvidia. Why? It's all due to the growth Nvidia will produce. During the company’s fiscal third quarter of 2027 (ending Oct. 25), CFO Colette Kress raised the company’s revenue growth guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% to 75%. That's an impressive figure considering how quickly Nvidia grew this year, and if those growth figures hold up, the stock will be even cheaper. Nvidia now trades for just 9.3 times next year's earnings. So, what's a fair value for Nvidia? If you think it's about 30 times trailing earnings, then if Nvidia rises to that level and hits next year's estimates, the stock could triple. A lot would need to go right with investigations, but it's not out of the question, either. While there are many unknowns about Nvidia's future, there are also many known factors. The AI boom isn't slowing down for anyone or anything, and that could lead to incredible performance over the next few years. I think now is the perfect time to buy Nvidia stock, as its price is driven more by fear than by reality. title: Anthropic’s Chip Choices Could Change the Nvidia Story. Here’s How. - The Motley Fool
content: Anthropic is spreading out its demand for AI accelerators across multiple companies. Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) made headlines recently because of its blockbuster IPO, and investors are still trying to decide how the newly public artificial intelligence (AI) company will impact the broader AI market. Some of the details Anthropic disclosed in its S-1 filing before going public shed light on its potential impact, especially on chip companies. Anthropic currently has deals with multiple chip companies to help provide the compute capacity it needs for its AI services. Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) is, unsurprisingly, a key supplier of chips to Anthropic, but so are Alphabet (GOOGL -2.13%) (GOOG -2.02%), Amazon (AMZN -3.12%), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.75%). Instead of tying itself to just one chip company, Anthropic has decided to spread out its chip vendors. That could change Nvidia's growth narrative in the coming years. Here's how it's shifting and why Nvidia investors don't need to panic just yet. Between cloud computing contracts and chip deals, Anthropic is on the hook for about $900 billion in spending over the next several years. That's a heck of a lot of money to spend, and Anthropic hopes it will accelerate its sales far beyond the company's current annual revenue run rate of $81 billion. It's also far too much money to funnel toward just one or two AI infrastructure companies. To minimize its supply chain risks, ensure it has the most advanced technology, and negotiate better chip prices, Anthropic spreads its chip deals across four key players. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,940,746 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. While Anthropic doesn't disclose all the details of each deal, including how much they might be worth, this data shows that Anthropic is clearly hedging its bets when it comes to buying AI chips. Nvidia's GPUs are still among the most in-demand chips in the world, and they're very likely to remain so for years to come due to AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia had an estimated 80%-90% market share of AI accelerators last year and is estimated to have 75% this year. That's both good and bad news for Nvidia. Having three-quarters of the AI accelerator market is huge, and it's part of the reason why Nvidia just reported another impressive quarter, with Q3 fiscal 2027 revenue rising 103% to $115.8 billion and earnings per share jumping 111% to $2.68. But AMD's GPUs and custom silicon from Google, Broadcom, and Amazon are reducing Nvidia's dominance. Part of the reason is that custom chips (like the ones Anthropic buys from Nvidia rivals) are good at handling agentic AI tasks and are more efficient than the raw processing power from GPUs. What's more, Nvidia's gross margins, while still high, are declining. The company said gross margins will be between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, down from nearly 75% in the third quarter. This downward pressure is mostly coming from rising memory costs right now, but intensifying chip competition could weigh on margins further in the coming years. Still, while Nvidia shareholders should be aware of how rival chip companies could impact the company over time, Nvidia is still the leading AI accelerator company. Its recent revenue guidance for 75% growth in the fourth quarter -- up from its previous guidance of 70% -- should reassure investors that the company isn't getting sidelined anytime soon. Michael Burry, the investor known for predicting the 2008 financial crisis, is sticking with his bearish view on Nvidia (NVDA). In a November 24 post on his Substack, Burry called the situation following Jensen Huang's return as president and CEO a "precarious normal." He also said his short thesis "is still valid, still has legs at full strength." At the same time, he disclosed buying more shares of Chinese companies JD.com (JD), Tencent (TCEHY), and BYD (BYDDF) as their share prices fell. Nvidia shares fell nearly 6% on Tuesday after surging 31% on Monday following news of Huang's return. However, Burry said his bearish view never depended on Huang leaving the company. Nvidia investors and the market in general reacted positively to news of the return of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry leader, who has been endorsed by none other than President Donald Trump himself. Yet, the legal troubles are far from over for the most famous leather jacket-clad executive in the world right now, specifically in Nvidia's home state of California. The Attorney General for the state of California recently revealed that Nvidia may be facing charges over possible violations of U.S. chip export rules. Announcing an investigation into the company, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said, "The basic legal framework that we're looking at is the prohibitions in California law — both civil and criminal — against misleading investors and the public. And there are multiple different laws that provide prohibitions in that space." Bonta noted that Nvidia could face financial penalties if found guilty, depending on "what was done, what the facts show, who knew what when, what the intent and state of mind was, and what the conduct was." As the excitement around Huang's return eventually dies down, investors should realize that the legal overhang around NVDA stock will continue to linger for a while. The company both directly and indirectly faces a number of investigations and inquiries involving federal agencies, national security matters, and congressional oversight. Last week, the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. Department of Justice confirmed an investigation into Megaspeed that began in 2024 after authorities identified suspicious activity involving potential semiconductor diversion. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list, but that reportedly did not stop the company from acquiring Nvidia chips after the fact. Meanwhile, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is reportedly investigating Nvidia's accounting amid concerns involving financing arrangements with AI customers and whether those arrangements could obscure revenue quality and financial exposure. Reportedly, the DOJ is also reviewing Nvidia's acquisitions, sales practices, customer pressure, and the possible tying of AI chips to networking equipment. Reporting on the matter has also referenced Nvidia's Hugging Face deal and Groq technology agreement. Finally, Congressional scrutiny is inevitable for Jensen Huang, who has agreed to appear before numerous House committees on Dec. 1. Notably, the political situation could also become considerably more difficult for Nvidia once Democrats take control of Congress in January. Remove all these legal tangles from Nvidia's fundamentals, however, and the financials appear as healthy as ever. Nvidia delivered another clean double beat and guidance that topped expectations in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. CFO Colette Kress also increased the company's revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2028 to 75% from the prior 70%. Revenue totaled $115.8 billion in Q3, marking a 103% increase from the year-ago period and exceeding consensus estimates. Data-center revenue advanced 110% year-over-year (YOY) to $107.6 billion, supported by a $20 billion contribution from the newest Vera Rubin rack-scale system, which management described as the fastest product ramp in the company's history. One key development during the quarter was Nvidia's decision to halt licensed Hopper GPU sales to China. Q4 revenue guidance of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, excluded any China Hopper contribution. On the earnings call, Kress outlined stricter limits on vendor financing. Guarantees will now be linked to measurable project progress, completion of required data-center infrastructure, and actual purchases and deployment of Nvidia equipment. The change reflects a measured approach from Kress — who has since returned to serving solely as CFO after a brief stint as interim CEO — particularly given the uncertain pace of data-center construction in the years ahead amid shifting political conditions. title: Jensen Huang Says Nvidia's Next-Gen Vera Rubin Chips Will Generate $40 Billion in Revenue per Gigawatt, Up From $25 Billion for Grace Blackwell. What That Means for NVDA's Growth Runway. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia isn't just achieving higher revenue per gigawatt through increased GPU selling prices. It's been an incredibly wild month for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) shareholders. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang and related dynamics kicked off a surge in selling action that saw the company's share price retreat 48% from the all-time high reached in early October. On Nov. 23, news that Huang had been reinstated as the CEO caused the company's share price to skyrocket 31.5% in a single trading session. The gains added nearly $1 trillion to the company's market capitalization, marking the largest single-day valuation gain for a company in history and spurring a wave of buying across the stock market that saw U.S. stocks rise by roughly $3 trillion. While Huang's return to Nvidia and the controversies over the smuggling of the company's export-banned chips to China will continue to be heavily discussed and debated in the near term, investors' focus will likely shift back to the company's actual business performance. Along those lines, Huang's estimates for the jump in monetization from the company's next-generation Vera Rubin processing platform look poised to play a powerful role in driving growth. After generating roughly $25 billion in revenue per gigawatt of compute with its Grace Blackwell platform, Huang sees the Vera Rubin platform generating $40 billion in sales per gigawatt -- good for a 60% increase. In addition to securing more revenue per gigawatt, Nvidia and its shareholders can also bet on a meaningful increase in the number of gigawatts of artificial intelligence (AI) compute as the data center build-out continues at a rapid pace. According to an estimate from Morgan Stanley, a Vera Rubin VR200 rack will set customers back roughly $7.8 million -- up from roughly $3.99 million for the GB300 rack. Other estimates suggest a lower price increase for the more capable, more energy-efficient racks, but more advanced processors and higher memory content are clearly set to facilitate substantial pricing and sales increases. On the other hand, more advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) and a greater number of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips aren't the only factors behind Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform delivering a big jump in sales per gigawatt compared to Blackwell. The company is also achieving the growth through its related Vera central processing units (CPUs) and new, internally developed networking hardware in its next-generation racks. Nvidia is seeing rapid growth in the CPU space and strong demand for Vera, and it expects that its total revenue from CPUs will more than double next year. The overall Vera Rubin platform provides a leap that bolsters Nvidia's edge in the AI compute space. In addition to simply generating more revenue per gigawatt, the performance jump provided by its newest GPUs and dramatic market share gains in the CPU category look poised to further strengthen the company's competitive position in the AI infrastructure market. title: Buy, Sell Or Hold Nvidia Stock After A 31.5% Day? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back? Nvidia stock rose 31.5% on Monday, Nov 23, to $165.05. It was its second-biggest one-day gain since 2003. On Friday it had fallen 14.0%. On Tuesday, Nov 24, it fell 5.9% to $155.38. So should you buy, sell or hold after a day like Monday? Nvidia’s own past gives a guide. After its 12 biggest days since 2003, the stock was higher a year later 10 times. But the biggest of them was followed by a 27.4% drop within three months. And Monday did not change the cash question behind our $92 floor, the price a fall could reach. Nvidia said on Monday that its board had reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. That came days after the board had said he would not return, The Wall Street Journal and CNBC reported. Its filing says the board received input from senior levels of the US government. The board’s own investigation continues. Chip stocks went with Nvidia. The chip ETF (SMH) rose 15.0%. Micron rose 19.0% and TSMC 14.1%. The S&P 500 (SPY) rose 4.7%. Take away the chip ETF’s gain, and about 16.5 points of Nvidia’s 31.5% were its own. Now look at the three days together. After Friday’s fall and Monday’s jump, Nvidia closed 1.4% above its Nov 13 close. After Tuesday’s 5.9% drop, it is 4.6% below. In our view, that is a round trip, not a rescue. Nvidia fell 14.0% on Friday, rose 31.5% on Monday and fell 5.9% on Tuesday. If you are waiting for calmer days to buy, your cash can earn something while you wait. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays. Trefis price data for Nvidia begins in December 2002. Since then, the stock has gained 15% or more in a day 12 times before Monday. The worst three months after any of those days was a 27.4% drop. It followed the biggest day of all. Source: Trefis, prices through Nov 24. Returns include dividends. The table shows the eight biggest days. The median covers all 12. The four days not shown were in October 2008, May 2016, March 2020 and February 2024. After each one, Nvidia was higher three and 12 months later. Their 12-month gains ran from 49.9% to 230.1%. Did a big day mean the worst was over? Usually, but not always. Twelve months later, Nvidia was higher 10 times out of 12. One month later, it was higher 9 times. The two that were lower a year later were both in 2003. And the biggest day of all came just before a 27.4% fall. So a big day pointed to gains a year out. It did not show how low the stock could go first. The data points two ways from Tuesday’s close. If Nvidia matched the median three months, +22.5%, it would be near $190 by late February. If it repeated May 2003, it would be near $113 by then. That is below Friday’s close. Below that sits the $92 floor from our Monday piece, Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92? It looked at six well-known cases of SEC accounting scrutiny since 2012. Four of those stocks were lower a year later. The two that held up took in about $1.80 of operating cash for every $1 of profit. Operating cash is the cash a business brings in from its day-to-day work. For Nvidia, the figure is 70 cents. Did Monday change the cash? No. A reinstated CEO and a 31.5% day do not change how much of each $1 of profit arrives as cash. That is the test in Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash. Two things would change the picture. One is a results report with operating cash back above profit. The other is the SEC examination Reuters reported ending with nothing to restate. One answer is to use the big day to rebalance, by a set rule. That means selling a stock back down to its target size when it grows past it. Say Nvidia was a $100,000 target position in a $2 million portfolio on Friday. After Monday it was worth about $131,500. After Tuesday it was about $123,800. Trimming back to target at Tuesday’s close banks about $23,800. Now say the stock fell to the $92 floor. The $100,000 position would lose about $40,800. That is 2.0% of the portfolio. In our view, a holder can survive that. Does the trim cost anything? Usually, yes. Say Nvidia matched the median year after a big day, a gain of 84.5%. Then the $23,800 would have grown to about $43,900. So the rule gives up about $20,100. That is the price of being able to survive a fall to the floor. Nvidia’s biggest days were usually followed by more gains, but the biggest was followed by a 27.4% drop. Investors changed their minds on Monday. Nvidia’s cash did not change. One stock can swing that hard in a single day. Owning many strong companies means no single stock decides how you do. title: NVDA Eyes Worst Month Since 2022 — Dip Buyers Are ‘Still Fighting To Break Even’ After Huang’s Return, Analyst Says - TradingView
content: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO added more than $952 billion to Nvidia’s market value on Monday. Yet, for retail investors who spent November buying the stock as it fell, the over 30% rally barely brought the average position back to even, market analyst Stephen Innes said, citing Vanda Research. NVDA stock slid 24% so far in November, on track to record its second straight month in the red. “There is an old trading-desk distinction between making money and recovering losses. Monday was largely a celebration of the latter,” Innes said. Retail investors bought a net $3.49 billion of Nvidia shares from Nov. 4 through Monday, but the payoff depended on when they bought. Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, said Nvidia’s dip buyers were “still fighting to break even” in his analysis of Vanda Research data. “There is an old trading-desk distinction between making money and recovering losses. Monday was largely a celebration of the latter,” he said. Buyers who stepped in during Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 fared better. They put in a net $1.12 billion at an estimated average price of $148.40 per share. “We estimate that the average retail investor who bought NVDA shares last week is up around 11% today (from being down 15% at Friday’s close),” Vanda said. By Tuesday’s close, that gain had narrowed to 4.7% for those who held on. Many earlier buyers were still in the red even after Monday’s rally, according to Vanda. Retail traders also concentrated their bets. Outside Nvidia and Anthropic, they sold more individual stocks than they bought in 10 of the previous 13 sessions. Meanwhile, SOXL, a fund targeting three times a semiconductor index’s daily return, drew a net $1.25 billion over the latest one-month period, the most in Vanda’s nine years of data. When Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, traders who had bet against tech stocks rushed to buy back shares to limit their losses. “Sometimes it simply means too many traders were short, liquidity was thin, and an unexpected catalyst forced everyone through the same door at once,” said Innes. Pompliano Says AI Demand Is ‘Still Outstripping Supply’ Investor Anthony Pompliano saw Nvidia’s rally as a vote for Jensen Huang and urged him to replace the board that forced him out. He also expects AI demand to keep pushing stocks higher. “The recent market sell-off gave everyone time to take a deep breath, but demand is still outstripping supply, so we are going much higher,” he said. Even by Cathie Wood’s ARK estimates, OpenAI and Anthropic more than tripled the capacity they used to answer customer requests over the past year, and revenue per gigawatt still rose. “The market seems to be afraid of its own shadow,” the firm said. “Historically, fearful markets have provided savvy investors with excellent entry points. ARK suspects that the same is true today.” Morningstar said Huang’s return makes Nvidia more likely to back smaller AI cloud providers and helps customers count on its next chips arriving on schedule. Export restrictions still cloud sales to Southeast Asian markets where operators rented computing power to Chinese AI developers. “We don’t believe that Nvidia is back to even with the start of the saga,” the firm said. Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to bring Huang back after consulting senior U.S. officials. It said his return posed no national security risk, while its independent investigation into reports that foreign intelligence had targeted him would continue. Huang is expected to testify before Congress next week. President Donald Trump reportedly said he would consider a pardon if necessary, but he thinks Huang would be fine without one. Meanwhile, AI researcher Gary Marcus pointed to a warning sign for OpenAI’s IPO ambitions. Even after Huang’s return, Anthropic and SpaceX were trading below their offer prices. “If those two stocks stay below their IPO price (or just hover near it, without significant gains), it’s difficult to imagine OpenAI IPOing at anything like the numbers they once envisioned,” he said. He added that a delayed listing could also hurt Nvidia, CoreWeave and Nebius. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for NVDA slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ levels a day ago amid ‘high’ message volume. One user saw an upside to the scrutiny in Washington, saying, “DC will just bring attention to how innovative $NVDA is.” Another user focused on how Nvidia’s customers fund their purchases. “the chip buyer is borrowing more to keep buying. that is a credit chain, not just demand,” the user said. So far this year, NVDA has fallen 17%, the steepest decline among the “Magnificent Seven,” while TSLA has dropped 14%, GOOGL and META have each lost 11%, and AAPL, AMZN and MSFT have gained 30%, 9% and 3%, respectively. title: Nvidia Is Down 31% From Its Peak. History Says This Happens Next - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia rebounded incredibly the last time it saw a steep pullback. Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) reached a 52-week high on Oct. 6, but they have dropped by a remarkable 31% since then, as investors pressed the panic button for multiple reasons. Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's resignation (before he was reinstated on Nov. 23), an investigation into Nvidia's dealings in China, and a reported probe by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) into the company's accounting practices have sent the stock packing over the past month and a half. The negativity surrounding Nvidia stock was so severe that even its quarterly results and better-than-expected guidance didn't arrest its slide. However, Nvidia rallied over 31% following Huang’s reappointment, suggesting that investor confidence in the stock could improve. What’s more, the last time Nvidia witnessed such a sharp pullback in a short period, it went on a multi-year rally. Let's take a look at what happened in 2018. Nvidia stock fell 54% between October and December 2018. This massive slide was triggered by an oversupply in the graphics processing unit (GPU) market, driven by a drop in cryptocurrency-related sales. Additionally, the company was caught up in a broader sell-off of tech stocks at the time. Nvidia's growth slowed as crypto-driven GPU demand faded, leaving the company with excess inventory. In fact, Nvidia's revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2019 (which ended in January 2019) fell 24% year over year to $2.2 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings dropped by 53% from the year-ago period during the quarter. Investors decided to book profits in Nvidia stock following stellar returns in 2016 and 2017. Nvidia lost 31% of its value in 2018. For comparison, it jumped by 227% in 2016 and 82% in 2017. So, this isn't the first time that Nvidia stock has lost its wheels and undergone a significant correction in a short time. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,940,746 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. However, what's worth noting is that Nvidia went on a stunning bull run starting in 2019, driven by multiple catalysts, including strong GPU sales during the novel coronavirus pandemic and the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in late 2022. Nvidia stock has jumped by a whopping 4,740% since the beginning of 2019. So, savvy investors who saw the long-term opportunity in Nvidia's shares at that time are sitting on massive gains right now, even after the stock's recent sell-off. What's more, a closer look at Nvidia's valuation suggests that it is way more attractive right now than it was in 2018. Nvidia traded at less than 18 times earnings at the end of 2018. The stock currently has a price-to-earnings ratio of 17.7, close to the level it traded at eight years ago. The forward earnings multiple of just 10 suggests that Nvidia is on track to deliver healthy bottom-line growth. Meanwhile, the stock's price/earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio was just 0.31 at the end of 2018. This is a forward-looking valuation metric that's calculated by dividing a stock's trailing earnings multiple by the projected annual earnings per share (EPS) growth over the long run, let's say for five years. A PEG ratio below 1 means that the stock is undervalued when its growth potential is considered. So, Nvidia was significantly undervalued at that time, just like it is right now. The stock currently has a PEG ratio of just 0.19, which means that investors are getting an even better deal than in 2018. But should they take this opportunity to buy shares given recent developments at the company? Investors are most likely in a classic dilemma right now. Nvidia's valuation suggests that the stock is a screaming buy, especially given its solid fundamentals, healthy growth, and sunny prospects. The company reported impressive year-over-year revenue growth of 103% in the third quarter of fiscal 2027 to $115.8 billion. Adjusted earnings per share shot up by 111% to $2.68. The numbers easily exceeded consensus EPS expectations of $2.48 and the $109.1 billion revenue estimate. The company expects $130 billion in revenue in the current quarter, a 91% jump over last year and well ahead of the $125.1 billion Wall Street estimate. Notably, analysts have raised their EPS expectations for Nvidia, indicating continued confidence in the company's prospects. So, investors with a higher risk appetite who have investable cash after paying their bills, clearing expensive loans, and saving for a rainy day can consider buying this semiconductor stock. That's because Nvidia could go on a massive bull run, fueled by Huang’s comeback and the solid growth that it is poised to deliver, which could lead the market to reward it with a higher valuation in the future. After all, Nvidia sees tremendous opportunity in the AI infrastructure market, and it is making solid progress in emerging niches, such as physical AI. However, the ongoing regulatory troubles the company faces suggest it may be wise for conservative investors to wait on the sidelines. content: Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire? Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, Nov 23. The stock rose 31.5% that day, to $165.05. It was Nvidia‘s third-largest one-day gain since 1999. That one session won back 82.0% of the 27.7% fall from the Nov 11 close, the last before Huang resigned, to the Nov 20 close. Our read: the bounce alone is not a reason to sell. Nvidia’s own record says to plan for another drop, though. So the real choice is how much Nvidia you hold, not when you sell. After 10 past fast rebounds since 1999, Nvidia closed below the drop’s low at some point in the next year in 7. Yet it was higher a year later in 9 of the 10. A holder had to sit through the second fall to collect the gain. Nvidia’s board started an independent investigation on Sunday, Nov 8, after reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. On Thursday, Nov 12, Nvidia said Huang had resigned as CEO. He was out for 11 days, or seven trading sessions. Nvidia also reported results on Nov 17, inside that window. So not all of the fall can be tied to Huang. Over the seven sessions he was out, Advanced Micro Devices fell 23.2%, chipmaker TSMC fell 22.9% and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) fell 9.0%. Still, Nov 12, the day he resigned, hit Nvidia alone. It fell 4.3%, while Broadcom rose 5.5% and AMD rose 5.9%. Nvidia fell 27.7% in seven sessions and won back 82.0% in one. Even so, Nvidia remains 5.0% below its Nov 11 close. It is still 31.0% below its Oct 6 record close of $239.24. Huang’s return was Monday’s big market story, and this bounce is the latest turn in our AI storyline. We checked every case since 1999 under one rule. A drop is a close at least 25% below the highest close of the prior 10 sessions. A fast rebound is a close within five sessions of the low that wins back at least half of that fall. Prices are split-adjusted closes, without dividends. Nvidia had 33 such drops and 10 fast rebounds with a full year of data since. Measured from the Nov 6 close of $186.64, the drop was 32.7%, and Monday won back 64.7% of it. So a fast rebound has been a better sign than usual. Nine of the 10 cases came in 2000-2008, and only one, in March 2020, is recent. A different threshold would give a different count. No, its record is weaker. Since 1999, the Invesco QQQ Trust had 31 fast rebounds from drops of 10% or more. That bar is lower than the 25% used for Nvidia, so the two records are not like for like. The 1999-2002 crash drives that result. Of the 11 fast rebounds since 2003, QQQ was higher a year later after nine. Nvidia traded at 17.7 times trailing earnings at Monday’s close. Trailing earnings are the net profit of the four quarters through Oct 25, 2026, about $9.34 a share. Its price-to-earnings ratio has been lower on 2.0% or fewer of trading days since 2019. title: Nvidia Stock Just Had Its Best Day in Over a Decade. I'd Still Buy It Now. - The Motley Fool
content: The AI chip giant's shares climbed around a third in one session. Is it still a bargain? Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) said on Monday, Nov. 23, that it had brought back Jensen Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately. Shares surged on the news. As I write, the stock's up about 34% for the day, at roughly $168. That'd be its largest one-day climb in over two decades, based on Yahoo Finance's daily closing prices. It'd also add about $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value in one session. But the stock sits around 30% below Oct. 6, when it closed at a record $239.24. And I think Nvidia is still cheap for what it's expected to earn, especially with Huang back and sales rising faster than a year ago. Huang stepped down on Nov. 11, after what Nvidia's board called personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct. Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and the board started looking for a permanent replacement. Six days later, when Nvidia posted fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones opened the earnings call by ruling out a return. "The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,940,746 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The selling kept going. Shares lost around 28% between the Nov. 11 close and Friday, Nov. 20, when the stock dropped 14% in one day. This was Nvidia's seventh straight losing week, its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. Five days after the call, the board reversed itself. Nvidia said its directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after a series of meetings with him. The board also said it got input from senior levels of the U.S. government before deciding. Sure, not everything is settled. A committee of independent directors is still investigating, and Nvidia said it'll keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Highlighting how strong demand stayed through all this, Nvidia's revenue surged 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in its fiscal 2027 third quarter, which ended on Oct. 25, 2026. Sales grew 20% from the previous quarter, a pickup from 18% sequential growth in fiscal Q2. What's more, earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis gained 111% year over year to $2.68, so profits more than kept up with sales. Management sees around $130 billion in revenue for fiscal Q4, a period with an extra week. Kress also said on the call that Vera Rubin, Nvidia's latest computing platform, pulled in almost $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. And she lifted Nvidia's outlook for next year, saying the company now expects fiscal 2028 revenue (the year ending in January 2028) to rise around 75%, up from its previous 70% forecast. In other words, the stock's drop after Huang's resignation was arguably about who would lead Nvidia, not about demand for its chips. With Huang back, much of that worry could fade. At roughly $168, Nvidia's stock price is about 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, based on analysts' average estimate. In comparison, shares of Advanced Micro Devices, one of Nvidia's top rivals in AI chips, cost about 26 times the company's expected 2027 earnings. Even after Monday's rally, then, investors are paying less than half as much for a dollar of Nvidia's expected profit. Nvidia is also buying back lots of its own stock. It returned $28.1 billion to shareholders in repurchases and dividends in fiscal Q3. And Kress said it still plans to spend the $227 billion or so left on its buyback authorization by the end of fiscal 2028 -- over 5% of Nvidia's market value at Monday's price. Yes, a price-to-earnings ratio this low only holds up if the earnings forecast does. Nvidia sees gross margin of 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, down from around 75% in fiscal Q3. And the board's investigation might still find something investors don't like. But at around 10 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, I'd say the stock already prices in a lot of bad news. In the end, Nvidia gets back the co-founder who ran it for more than three decades, and it gets him back with sales still more than doubling year over year. I'd still buy the stock after Monday's jump, but I'd likely add shares bit by bit over the next few months, given how volatile the stock is. There’s no guarantee it doesn’t go lower again.
